questions.stem: Given the sets A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {2, 3, 4}, prove that (A ∪ B) ∩ B = B.
questions.solution: The union of sets A and B (A ∪ B) is {1, 2, 3, 4}. When we intersect this with set B, we retain only the elements that are in both A ∪ B and B. Since B is already a subset of A ∪ B, the intersection results in B itself: (A ∪ B) ∩ B = {2, 3, 4} = B.
questions.explanation: This question tests understanding of set operations and how to prove set identities using their definitions.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake is to assume that the intersection will result in A ∪ B, which is not correct because we are intersecting with B.

questions.solution: The intersection of sets A and B (A ∩ B) contains elements that are in both A and B. When we union this with set A, we add any elements from A that were not in the intersection but already exist in A: (A ∩ B) ∪ A = A.
questions.explanation: This question tests understanding of set operations and how to prove set identities using their definitions.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake is to assume that the union will result in B or A ∪ B, which is not correct because we are starting with elements from A.

questions.stem: Given the sets X = {x | x is a prime number less than 10} and Y = {y | y is an even prime number}, prove that X ∩ Y = {}.
questions.solution: The set X contains prime numbers less than 10, which are {2, 3, 5, 7}. The set Y contains even prime numbers, which is just {2}. Since there is only one even prime number and it is also in X, but no other elements in X are even, the intersection of X and Y is empty: X ∩ Y = {}.
questions.explanation: This question tests understanding of set operations and how to prove set identities using specific examples.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake is to assume that X ∩ Y = {2}, which is not correct because even though 2 is in both sets, it is the only element in Y.

questions.stem: Prove that (A ∪ B) ∆ A = (A - B) ∪ (B - A), where ∆ denotes the symmetric difference.
questions.solution: The symmetric difference (A ∆ B) of sets A and B contains elements that are in either A or B, but not both. When we take the symmetric difference of (A ∪ B) with A, we remove any elements that are only in A: (A ∪ B) ∆ A = (A - B) ∪ (B - A).
questions.explanation: This question tests understanding of set operations and how to prove set identities using their definitions.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake is to assume that the symmetric difference will result in A ∩ B or A ∪ B, which is not correct because we are removing elements from A that are also in (A ∪ B).

questions.stem: Given the sets P = {1, 2, 3, 4} and Q = {3, 4, 5, 6}, prove that (P - Q) ∩ Q = {}.
questions.solution: The set difference (P - Q) contains elements that are in P but not in Q, which is {1, 2}. When we intersect this with set Q, we find no elements that are in both sets: (P - Q) ∩ Q = {}.
questions.explanation: This question tests understanding of set operations and how to prove set identities using specific examples.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake is to assume that (P - Q) ∩ Q contains elements from P, which is not correct because we are only considering elements in P that are not in Q.

questions.stem: Prove that if A ⊆ B, then A ∪ C = B ∪ C for any set C.
questions.solution: If set A is a subset of set B (A ⊆ B), then all elements of A are also in B. When we union either set with another set C, the result will be the same because the elements from A are already included in B: A ∪ C = B ∪ C.
questions.explanation: This question tests understanding of set containment and how it affects set operations.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake is to assume that A ∪ C ≠ B ∪ C, which is not correct because the elements from A are already in B when A ⊆ B.

questions.stem: Given the sets R = {x | x is a real number} and S = {x | x is an irrational number}, prove that R ∩ S = S.
questions.solution: The intersection of the set of all real numbers (R) and the set of irrational numbers (S) is just the set of irrational numbers because every irrational number is also a real number: R ∩ S = S.
questions.explanation: This question tests understanding of set operations and how to prove set identities using specific examples.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake is to assume that R ∩ S = R, which is not correct because the intersection only includes irrational numbers, not all real numbers.
